title: Views & Surface Area — Practice
intro: Every question from the slides (Together and Your turn), with a hands-on lab after you solve each one. Do them on paper first, then check here.

questions.title: Views of a Stack — how many cubes?
questions.text: The **stack plan** is the view from above, with a number in every square. The number tells you how many cubes are stacked there — **including the cubes you cannot see in the picture**. How many cubes are in this stack?
hints: Look at the numbers in the stack plan. What does the **3** in the middle square tell you?
A square marked 2 holds 2 cubes, a square marked 0 holds none. So add up the nine numbers.

traps.0: 7 counts the **squares that have cubes** (7 stacks). But a stack marked 3 is three cubes, not one.
traps.1: 9 counts all nine squares of the 3 × 3 base. The numbers say how **tall** each square is — add them, don’t count the squares.
traps.3: 13 comes from adding the squares of the front view and the right view (6 + 7). A view only shows the **tallest** stack in each line of sight, so its squares are not a cube count.

solution: Every number is a stack height, so add them all: 2 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 0 + 2 + 1 = **11**.
Check layer by layer from the bottom: the bottom layer has 7 cubes, the middle layer 3, the top layer 1 → 7 + 3 + 1 = **11**.
questions.idea: The stack plan tells the true height of every square — add the numbers.

hints: A view shows the **tallest stack** in each line of sight. For the front view, look at one **column** of the plan at a time.
Front view, left to right: column 1 (2, 1, 0) → 2, column 2 (1, 3, 2) → 3, column 3 (0, 1, 1) → 1.
Right view: look at one **row** at a time, starting with the **front** row (0 2 1 → 2), then the middle row (1 3 1 → 3), then the back row (2 1 0 → 2).

traps.0: This front view is a mirror image (1, 3, 2). The front view starts with the **left** column of the plan — that column’s tallest stack is 2.
traps.2: You swapped the two views. The **front** view is made from the **columns** of the plan (2, 3, 1); the **right** view is made from its **rows** (2, 3, 2).
traps.3: That front view copies just the **front row** (0 2 1). The front view looks along every row, so each column shows its tallest stack — the 2 in the back row counts too.

solution: Front view = tallest stack of each column, left to right: **2, 3, 1**.
Right view = tallest stack of each row, front row first: **2, 3, 2**.
The pair with front 2-3-1 and right 2-3-2 is the answer.
questions.idea: Front view: columns, left to right. Right view: rows, front row on the left.

questions.title: Counting a Staircase
questions.text: This staircase is built from identical cubes. How many cubes does it use? (Remember the cubes you cannot see.)
hints: Look at the picture from the side. Under each cube on a high step there are more cubes holding it up.
Count **layer by layer, from the bottom up**. How many cubes are in the bottom layer?
Bottom layer: 3 × 3 = 9. Second layer: two rows of 3. Top layer: one row of 3.

traps.0: 9 counts only the **top faces** you can see (3 on each step). Under each one there are more cubes.
traps.1: 12 is the number of cubes you can **see** in the picture. The rest are hidden behind and under the higher steps — they are still part of the staircase.
traps.3: 27 would fill a whole 3 × 3 × 3 cube. But the front steps are lower, so there are empty spaces above them.

solution: Count layer by layer from the bottom: bottom layer 3 × 3 = **9**, second layer 2 rows × 3 = **6**, top layer 1 row × 3 = **3**.
Shortcut: three rows with 1, 2 and 3 cubes in each column: (1 + 2 + 3) × 3 = 18.
questions.idea: Count layer by layer from the bottom up — hidden cubes count too.

questions.title: What Is the Most Cubes?
questions.text: A stack stands on a **3 × 3 base**. Its front view and right view are shown (in the right view the front row is on the left). What is the **largest** number of cubes the stack could contain?
hints: To get the **most** cubes, fill every square as high as **both** views allow.
A square in column 1 and the front row: the front view allows 3, the right view allows 2. Use the smaller number.
Row by row, front row first: 2 + 1 + 2, then 3 + 1 + 2, then 1 + 1 + 1.

traps.0: 6 is the **fewest** cubes that still show these views. This question asks for the largest.
traps.1: 12 adds the squares of the two views (6 + 6). A view is not a pile of separate cubes — one cube can show up in both views.
traps.3: 27 would fill the whole 3 × 3 × 3 box. But column 2 of the front view is only 1 tall, and the back row of the right view is only 1 tall.

solution: Each square can be only as tall as **both** views allow: the smaller of its column height and its row height.
Front row (right view says 2): min(3,2) + min(1,2) + min(2,2) = 2 + 1 + 2 = **5**.
questions.idea: Views set a ceiling. Most cubes: fill every square as high as BOTH views allow.

questions.title: Staircase Corner — (a) how many cubes?
questions.text: (a) How many cubes make this stack?
hints: Some cubes are hidden under the taller stacks. Count **layer by layer from the bottom**.
The bottom layer is a triangle of cubes: 3 + 2 + 1.
Bottom layer 6, middle layer 3, top layer 1.

traps.0: 6 counts the cubes you can **see** (one top each). The taller stacks have cubes hidden underneath them.

solution: Bottom layer: 3 + 2 + 1 = **6** cubes.
Middle layer: 2 + 1 = **3** cubes.
Top layer: **1** cube.
questions.idea: Count layer by layer, from the bottom up.

Front view, left to right: the left column is the tallest (3), then 2, then 1.
In the **right** view the **front** row is on the left, and the front row is only 1 tall.

traps.0: Both views are mirrored. The front view starts at the **left** of the stack, where the tallest column is; the right view starts at the **front**, where it is lowest.
traps.1: The front view is right, but in the **right** view the front row goes on the left — and the front row is the lowest (1).
traps.3: The right view is right, but the front view starts with the **left** column, which is the tallest (3).

solution: Front view (columns, left to right): **3, 2, 1**.
Right view (rows, front row first): **1, 2, 3**.

questions.title: George’s Cross
questions.text: George built the shape shown using seven unit cubes. How many such cubes does he have to add to make a cube with edges of length 3?
hints: How many unit cubes make a cube with edges of length 3? Think about layers.
Each layer is 3 × 3 = 9 cubes, and there are 3 layers.

traps.1: 14 is 7 + 7 — doubling what George already has. The finished cube is **3 × 3 × 3**, which has more cubes than that.

solution: A cube with edges of length 3 is made of 3 × 3 × 3 = **27** unit cubes.
George has 7, so he needs 27 − 7 = **20** more.
Check by layers: the top layer has 1 cube (needs 8 more), the middle layer has 5 (needs 4 more), the bottom layer has 1 (needs 8 more): 8 + 4 + 8 = 20.
questions.idea: Fill the big cube: total − what you already have.

questions.text: A teacher puts a square table next to a shaded circle drawn on the floor. She divides the table into nine squares numbered 1 to 9 (see the picture). She then stacks equal cubes on the squares: **2** cubes on square 8, **3** on square 2, **1** on square 6 and **4** on square 1. questions.title: Irene’s City
questions.text: Irene made a “city” with identical wooden cubes. One diagram shows the view from above the city (shaded squares have cubes) and the other the view from one of the sides. **It is not known from which side** the side view was taken. What is the largest number of cubes that Irene could have used?
hints: The side view could have been taken from any of the **four edges** of the top view. Try each one.
From each edge, the side view gives a height to every line of sight. To get the most cubes, make **every** shaded square as tall as its line allows.
Count the shaded squares in each column (3, 1, 2, 3) and in each row (2, 2, 2, 3), then pair them with the heights 2, 4, 1, 3 in both orders.

traps.0: 25 is not possible: the four edges give 21, 22, 23 and 24 cubes. Try them all and take the largest.
traps.2: 23 is the total when the side view is taken from the **left** edge — a real possibility, but not the largest.
traps.3: 22 is the total when the side view is taken from the **right** edge — real, but not the largest.
traps.4: 21 is what you get if the side view is read from the **bottom** edge in the order given. Other edges give more — try them all.

solution: Shaded squares per column (left to right): 3, 1, 2, 3. Per row (top to bottom): 2, 2, 2, 3. Side view heights: 2, 4, 1, 3.
From the bottom edge (heights match the columns in order): 3×2 + 1×4 + 2×1 + 3×3 = 21. From the top edge (reversed): 3×3 + 1×1 + 2×4 + 3×2 = **24**.
From the left edge (match the rows in order): 2×2 + 2×4 + 2×1 + 3×3 = 23. From the right edge (reversed): 2×3 + 2×1 + 2×4 + 3×2 = 22.
The largest possible is **24**.
questions.idea: When one fact is unknown, try every possibility and keep the best.

questions.title: Surface Area of a Box
questions.text: Find the surface area of this rectangular box (5 cm long, 3 cm wide, 4 cm high).
hints: A box has 6 faces in 3 matching pairs: top & bottom, front & back, left & right.
Find the area of one face from each pair, then **double** each.

traps.0: 47 is half the answer: it adds only **one** face from each pair. Every face has a partner on the opposite side — double it.
traps.1: 60 is the **volume** (5 × 3 × 4, in cm³). Surface area is the total area of the six faces, in cm².

solution: Top & bottom: 2 × (5 × 3) = 30.
Front & back: 2 × (5 × 4) = 40.
Left & right: 2 × (3 × 4) = 24.
questions.idea: Find each pair of faces — then double.

questions.title: Glued Cubes
questions.text: Five cubes with edge 1 cm are glued together as shown (four in a 2 × 2 square, one more on top of the back cube). What is the surface area of the solid?
hints: Five separate cubes would have 5 × 6 = 30 faces. Gluing hides some of them.
Every glued joint hides **2** faces — one on each cube. How many joints are there?
Joints: 4 in the bottom 2 × 2 square, plus 1 where the top cube sits.

traps.0: 10 counts only the faces you can **see** in the picture. Faces at the back, underneath and on the hidden sides count too.
traps.2: 25 treats each joint as hiding **one** face. A joint touches two cubes, so it hides **two** faces.
traps.3: 30 is 5 × 6 — it ignores the glue completely.

solution: 5 cubes × 6 faces = **30** faces.
Glued joints: 4 around the 2 × 2 base + 1 under the top cube = **5**.
Each joint hides 2 faces: 30 − 2 × 5 = **20 cm²**.
Check by counting: top 4 + bottom 4 + front 3 + back 3 + left 3 + right 3 = 20 ✅
questions.idea: SA = 6n − 2 × (joints). Hidden faces do not count.

questions.source: Class slides — Surface Area · Your turn 1
questions.title: From Volume to Surface Area
questions.text: A cube has volume **125 cm³**. What is its surface area?
hints: For a cube, volume = edge × edge × edge. Which number gives 125 when you multiply it by itself three times?
The edge is 5 cm.
A cube has 6 identical square faces: SA = 6 × edge².

traps.0: 25 is the area of **one** face (5 × 5). A cube has six faces.
traps.1: 30 is 6 × 5 — the edge was not squared. Each face is 5 × 5 = 25 cm².
traps.2: 125 is the **volume** (in cm³). Surface area is the area of the six faces (in cm²).

solution: 5 × 5 × 5 = 125, so the edge is **5 cm**.
One face: 5 × 5 = 25 cm².
Six faces: 6 × 25 = **150 cm²**.
questions.idea: Cube: V = s³ and SA = 6s². Find the edge first.

questions.source: Class slides — Surface Area · Your turn 2
questions.title: Cubes in a Row
questions.text: Three cubes with edge **2 cm** are glued face to face in a row. What is the surface area of the solid?

explorer.extra: Here the cubes have edge 1 and the row has surface area 14. Make every edge **2 times longer** → every area is **2² = 4 times** bigger: 14 × 4 = 56.

hints: One cube with edge 2 cm has surface area 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cm². Three separate cubes: 72 cm². Now take away the hidden faces.
There are **2** glued joints. Each joint hides **2** faces of 2 × 2 = 4 cm².

traps.0: 48 forgets the two **end** squares: the long sides give 4 × (2 × 6) = 48, but the two ends add 2 × 4 = 8 more.
traps.2: 64 treats each joint as hiding only **one** face (72 − 2 × 4). A joint hides **two** faces, one on each cube.
traps.3: 72 ignores the glue: 3 × 24 counts the hidden faces too.

solution: Separate cubes: 3 × 24 = 72 cm².
Joints: 2. Each hides 2 faces of 4 cm² → 2 × 2 × 4 = 16 cm² hidden.
questions.idea: Count every face, then take away the hidden ones (2 per joint).

questions.title: A 1 × 2 × 2 Prism
questions.text: What is the surface area of a 1 cm by 2 cm by 2 cm rectangular prism?
hints: Find the three pairs of faces. Two of the dimensions are 2 and one is 1.
Top & bottom are 2 × 2 squares. The four sides are 1 × 2 rectangles.

traps.3: 24 treats it like a 2 × 2 × 2 cube (6 faces of 4 cm²). The height is only 1 cm, so four of the faces are 1 × 2 = 2 cm².

solution: Top & bottom: 2 × (2 × 2) = 8.
Front & back: 2 × (2 × 1) = 4.  Left & right: 2 × (2 × 1) = 4.
questions.idea: Find each pair of faces — then double.

questions.title: Stretching a Prism
questions.text: The volume of a rectangular prism is 30 cm³. The length of the prism is doubled, the width is tripled, and the height is divided by four. The volume of the new prism is
hints: Volume = length × width × height. If each side is changed, the volume is changed by all three factors multiplied together.
Doubling the length → × 2. Tripling the width → × 3. Dividing the height by four → × ¼.
2 × 3 × ¼ = 1.5. So the new volume is 30 × 1.5.

traps.1: 120 = 30 × 4. But dividing the height by four makes the volume **smaller** in that direction, so the factor is ¼, not 4.
traps.2: 60 only uses the doubling (× 2). The width is tripled and the height is divided by four as well.
traps.3: 90 only uses the tripling (× 3). The length is doubled and the height is divided by four as well.

solution: Volume = l × w × h, so the new volume = old volume × 2 × 3 × ¼.
questions.idea: Scaling: every side change multiplies the volume. Multiply the factors, then multiply the old volume.

questions.title: Cutting the Corners
questions.text: From a wooden cube with side 3 cm we cut out at the corner a little cube with side 1 cm (see picture). What is the number of **faces** of the solid after cutting out such a small cube at **each corner** of the big cube?
hints: The cube starts with 6 faces. What happens to each of those faces when a corner is cut off?
Each original face just gets notched — it is still **one** face. But each cut also makes **3 new** little faces inside the notch.
8 corners × 3 new faces, plus the 6 original faces.

traps.2: 24 counts only the **new** faces (8 × 3). The 6 original faces are still there — notched, but still one face each.

solution: A cube has **6** faces. After the cuts, each of them still counts as one face (with notches in its corners).
Each cut-out corner adds **3** new faces (the three little squares of the notch).
8 corners × 3 = 24 new faces.
questions.idea: Count the old faces that survive, then add the new ones.

questions.title: Tilting the Water Box
questions.text: A closed rectangular prism with height 8 cm is standing on a face with dimensions 2 cm by 5 cm. The prism contains water with a depth of 6 cm. When the prism is tipped so that it stands on the face with the **greatest area**, the depth of the water is
hints: Tilting a closed box does not change the **volume of water** inside. Find that volume first.
The faces of the box: 2 × 5, 2 × 8 and 5 × 8. Which has the greatest area?
Depth = water volume ÷ area of the face it stands on.

traps.0: 0.75 is 6 ÷ 8: scaling the old depth by the height. But it is the **volume** of water that stays the same, not the depth.

solution: Water volume = 2 × 5 × 6 = **60 cm³** (it does not change when the box is tipped).
The three faces have areas 2 × 5 = 10, 2 × 8 = 16 and 5 × 8 = 40. The greatest is **40 cm²**.
questions.idea: Water volume stays the same: depth = volume ÷ base area.
